g.passage: When the buffet doors opened, the wedding hall in Busan dissolved into a hundred conversations, and Sunja let the noise carry her to a corner table. Joon, her grandson, slid in beside her, tugging at a collar his mother had ironed too stiffly, and teased her about the cousin who had tripped on the aisle runner. Sunja swatted his wrist and laughed until her eyes watered. Then he drew a creased photograph from his jacket: a young woman in a borrowed hanbok beside a man no one in the family had ever named. "Who is he, Halmeoni?" Sunja glanced at it, smiled, and said it was only a neighbor, a long time ago. She refilled Joon's cup, though it was nearly full, and asked loudly whether he had tried the japchae. Twice more she praised the bride's dress. When he slid the photograph back toward her, she placed her napkin over it, smoothing the cloth flat with both hands, and turned to wave at a cousin across the room.

g.passage: Who goes to the cinema in Tromso in May, when the sun refuses to set and no one needs the dark? Anders asked himself this as he bought a ticket from a girl reading a magazine. Inside, the theater held eleven people, and one of them was Anneke, who had not come to Mass in three years. She waved with easy warmth, and Anders, who had rehearsed several gentle reproaches over the years, found he wanted none of them. They traded complaints about the stale popcorn and the price of parking. Then Anneke's daughter leaned across her mother's lap. "Why don't we go to church anymore? You said Father Anders moved away." Anneke laughed a little too quickly and said children mix everything up. Anders laughed as well, and agreed that he did travel a great deal. He began folding his ticket stub into smaller and smaller squares. When the lights finally dimmed, he found himself studying the advertisements with unusual care.

g.passage: Kagiso never hurried. At the rural post office he stood at the counter with his hat in his hands while the clerk weighed a parcel of seed catalogs, and he answered every question about the rain twice. Marcus, the surveyor from Cape Town, waited behind him with a loan document that needed the farmer's signature before the afternoon bus, tapping the paper against his leg. The clerk, counting stamps, remarked that Kagiso's late wife had run this counter for thirty years. Marcus barely heard. A minute later the clerk added that the brass scale had been hers, and that Kagiso came every week to have it checked, though he rarely mailed anything. Marcus looked at the weights, worn smooth at the handles. He thought of the six-month extension his office liked to call a favor, and he slid the document back into its folder. When Kagiso finally turned around, Marcus asked him about the rain. Outside, the bus driver honked once and pulled away down the gravel road.

g.passage: Bao did not like surprises. As captain of the river freighter, he had found Wira curled among the rice sacks two days out, and now, docked below the terraced hills outside Hanoi, he had brought the boy home to eat because there was nowhere else to put him. Bao's mother set out bowls and chopsticks with the precision she gave to every meal. Wira, from an island far to the south, hesitated, then began eating with his right hand as his family always had. Bao waited for the small frown he had known since childhood. Instead his mother watched a moment, set down her chopsticks, and tore a piece of rice cake with her fingers. Bao felt the meal tilt on its hinge. Later Wira picked up the chopsticks and fumbled a dumpling into his lap, and Bao's mother laughed, a sound Bao had not heard at that table in years. Mist gathered over the terraces, erasing the lower paddies one by one.

g.passage: Dakar's Corniche was nearly empty at dusk when Yuto and Kwesi locked the shutters of their radio-repair shop for what might be the last time. Their oldest friend lay in the hospital above the promenade, and at every visit they had described customers who did not exist, a backlog of sets, a new sign. At first his face had brightened at each report. Lately he only nodded and asked about the weather. Kwesi wanted to keep the story going; it cost them nothing, he said. Yuto walked beside him along the sea wall without answering. Their kindness, he thought, had become a lantern without oil, still lifted at the bedside every evening. He remembered how their friend had begun turning toward the window whenever the shop was mentioned. At the hospital stairs Yuto stopped and said he would tell the truth tonight. Kwesi looked at the sea before nodding. Fishermen were hauling their painted pirogues up the wet sand.

g.passage: Dario hung his uniforms on the rooftop line every morning at six, after our night shift at the bakery in Oaxaca, and I, Tendai, hung mine beside his. For months he had talked of quitting to drive a taxi with his cousin; he kept the license forms folded in his wallet and showed them to anyone who asked. That spring he showed them less often, and when he did, the creases had gone soft and gray. One morning I noticed he had begun pinning a second apron to the line, the white one the head baker gave only to those training for the ovens. He did not mention it, and neither did I. Weeks later, when I finally asked about the taxi, he shrugged and said his plans had gone out with the wash. He seemed neither sorry nor relieved, only mildly surprised, as though remembering a coat he had once owned. Below us the street vendors were unfolding their umbrellas, one stripe at a time.

g.passage: "Careful, that bow is older than both of us," Gunnar said, grinning, as Callum fumbled it beside the cafe's sugar bowl. Trains hissed beyond the Rotterdam windows, and the conductor teased the boy about his cold coffee and his crooked collar and the way he held a fork like a bow. Callum, emboldened, asked whose bow it had been. Gunnar kept smiling, but he did not answer at once. He turned the bow slowly in his hands, thumb resting on the worn grip where another thumb had pressed first. His teacher, he said, had played with it for forty years and left it to him without a note. He mentioned this lightly, as if it were a detail about train times, and then said nothing more for a while, watching the departures board flick through cities he had no plans to visit. g.passage: When I was nineteen, my stepfather and I worked the dark hours at Rivka's bakery in Haifa, shaping dough before the shutters rose. He had paid my first year of tuition, and neither of us ever spoke of it; I assumed the money had simply been there. For months I treated those mornings as a sentence to be served, sulking over the cold flour and his habit of humming off-key. One morning Rivka, counting the till, said she would miss him after the holidays, when he could finally stop doing doubles. I did not ask what she meant. But I began to notice how he flexed his cracked knuckles before lifting the trays, and how he ate standing up. A week later I arrived early and had the ovens lit before he came. He looked at them, then at me, and hummed the same tune, slightly less off-key.

g.passage: When Lachlan finally carried the tin box up the lighthouse stairs in Galway, I had not spoken to him in four years, and our mother had been gone for two. The letters inside were hers, written to us during the winters she kept the light alone, and never sent. I expected complaints; she had been a sharp, impatient woman, and I had left home partly to escape her. Some letters did complain, about the damp, about our father, about me. But between the complaints she described the gannets diving at dawn, the exact color of the sea before a storm, and the biscuits she hid in a drawer for visits that rarely came. Reading them aloud, Lachlan's voice cracked on a line about my handwriting, which she had apparently kept. I did not forgive her everything. I did ask him to read that one again. g.passage: Gdansk in late October smells of wet grass and shipyard diesel, and that is where Milena found me, on the bench beside the field my brothers once ruled.
